name: Biliopancreatic diversion with duodenal switch (BPD/DS)

card.summary: A bariatric operation that shrinks the stomach and reroutes the small intestine, producing large and lasting weight loss that changes body shape and facial fat for people with severe obesity.
card.note: Major abdominal surgery with lifelong vitamin and nutrient supplementation and monitoring needs.

quick.overview:
BPD/DS is a weight-loss operation for people with severe obesity. A sleeve gastrectomy permanently reduces stomach size, and the intestine is rerouted so food meets digestive juices only late in the gut. Surgical literature reports it as producing the largest and most durable weight loss of the common bariatric procedures.

In appearance terms, large fat loss reshapes the body and face, which is why it appears in the wiki's hard-maxx category. Randomised trials have compared it with gastric bypass in people with BMI above 50, and the operation carries significant nutritional risks that require lifelong follow-up.
quick.how: It is performed by a bariatric surgeon in hospital, usually in people with a high BMI, and is followed by permanent vitamin and mineral supplementation, protein-focused eating and regular blood tests. Resistance training and nutrition guidance are part of published post-surgery recommendations.
quick.risks: Risks include nutritional deficiencies (vitamins A, D, E, K, B12, iron, thiamine, folate), kidney stones, complications needing reoperation, and the general risks of abdominal surgery. Clinical guidelines recommend lifelong nutritional monitoring.

lead: Biliopancreatic diversion with duodenal switch (BPD/DS) is a bariatric procedure in which a sleeve gastrectomy leaves a smaller stomach and the small intestine is rearranged so that digestive fluids from the liver and pancreas join the food stream far down the gut.[1] It is a less common procedure than sleeve gastrectomy or gastric bypass, though its use is increasing.[1]

For appearance, its relevance is the amount of fat loss it produces. A 2019 systematic review summarised in Wikipedia gives an estimated weight loss of about 74% of excess weight for biliopancreatic bypass with or without duodenal switch, the highest of the procedures compared.[1] People who lose large amounts of weight see changes in face, jawline and body shape, which is why surgical weight loss is discussed alongside other body-change methods.

Research includes a randomised trial comparing duodenal switch with gastric bypass in super obesity with follow-up to 15 years,[2] trials comparing the single-anastomosis variant (SADI) with BPD/DS,[3] and the American clinical practice guidelines for nutrition around bariatric surgery.[4] Reported drawbacks include deficiencies in fat-soluble vitamins and calcium.[5][6]

angle.text: The operation reduces food intake and absorption, producing substantial weight loss in people with severe obesity. The resulting fat loss changes facial and body contours.

infobox: Scopinaro's biliopancreatic diversion; duodenal switch modification described in the 1990s[7]

paras: The surgeon first creates a sleeve-shaped stomach, then connects the stomach outlet to a distant part of the small intestine, forming an alimentary limb, and routes bile and pancreatic secretions to join it near the end of the intestine.[1] Weight loss is attributed to changes in gut hormones controlling hunger and fullness, reduced stomach capacity and reduced nutrient absorption.[1]

In 1990 Scopinaro's biliopancreatic diversion with distal gastrectomy was modified: a sleeve gastrectomy with duodenal switch replaced the distal gastrectomy and the common channel was lengthened from 50 cm to 100 cm.[7] Early laparoscopic experience, including a 40-patient case series, was published in 2000.[8]

Reviews report that bariatric surgery overall produces weight loss and improves diabetes, hyperlipidaemia, hypertension and sleep apnoea.[9] BPD/DS is reported to give greater and more lasting weight loss and diabetes resolution than sleeve gastrectomy or Roux-en-Y bypass.[1]

Deficiencies of vitamins A, D, E, K and B12, iron, thiamine and folate occur after bariatric surgery, with malabsorptive procedures causing fat-soluble vitamin and calcium abnormalities.[5][6][1] Kidney stone risk was about tenfold in one study of biliopancreatic diversion and around 5% required reoperation for complications.[1] Adherence to multivitamins after surgery has been reported to be below 20%.[1] Guidelines cover supplements, nutrition and physical activity before and after surgery.[4][10]

A randomised trial in super obesity followed duodenal switch and gastric bypass patients for 15 years.[2] Another randomised trial compared SADI with BPD/DS for perioperative safety and one-year outcomes,[3] and an exploratory randomised trial examined a long alimentary limb duodenal switch at two years.[11] A matched controlled trial studied duodenal switch with a 200 cm common channel.[12] Registered trials include comparisons of single-anastomosis and standard duodenal switch.[13]

timeline.event: Scopinaro's biliopancreatic diversion is modified into a sleeve gastrectomy with duodenal switch.[7]
A 40-patient laparoscopic BPD/DS case series is published.[8]
A JAMA meta-analysis reviews bariatric surgery outcomes.[9]
